notes.b: Protein is built from a small set of chemical elements, and one of them, nitrogen, is found in no other nutrient. This is what makes protein different from carbohydrate and fat.
points: Every protein contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Some proteins also contain small amounts of sulphur, phosphorus and iron.
Protein is the only nutrient that contains nitrogen. Carbohydrate and fat contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so they contain none. Nitrogen is the element essential for growth.
These elements are arranged into basic units called amino acids. A protein is a large molecule made of many amino acids joined together.
Nitrogen sits in the amino group (the –NH₂ part) of every amino acid, so the nitrogen in a food comes from its protein.
Sulphur is found in only some amino acids, such as cysteine and methionine, which is why only some proteins contain it.
notes.tip: If asked to name the four elements in protein, give carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and say nitrogen is the one found only in protein. Expect true/false statements too: proteins are large molecules made of amino acids (true), and protein is the only nutrient containing nitrogen (true).

notes.h: Basic structure of an amino acid
notes.b: Every amino acid has the same central carbon atom bonded to four groups. Only the side group differs between amino acids, and that difference is what makes each one unique.
points: An amino group, –NH₂, which carries the nitrogen. It is basic (alkaline).
A carboxyl group, –COOH, which is the acidic part of the amino acid.
A hydrogen atom.
A variable side group, written R. It differs between amino acids and gives each one its identity. R is a group of atoms, not an element.
The body builds its proteins from about 20 different amino acids. Different proteins are different sequences of the same 20, much as different words are made from the same letters.
Diagram: draw a central carbon bonded to H, R, –COOH and –NH₂. Label each group, naming the amino group (–NH₂), the carboxyl group (–COOH) and R as the side group that varies.
notes.tip: When asked to complete the amino acid diagram, label the amino (–NH₂) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups. Students often swap them: the amino group has the nitrogen, and the carboxyl group is the acid.

notes.h: Essential and non-essential amino acids (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The body can make some amino acids itself but not others. Those it cannot make have to arrive in food, which is why the idea matters for diet.
points: Essential (indispensable) amino acids cannot be made by the body, or not in adequate amounts, so they must be supplied by the diet. Lysine is an example.
Eight amino acids are essential for adults: lysine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine and tryptophan.

Children also need histidine and arginine, which makes ten essential amino acids for children. Give the figures of eight for adults and ten for children; if a question gives nine, accept it, since some sources count histidine as essential for adults too.
Non-essential amino acids can be made by the body from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds, so food does not need to supply them.
Examples of non-essential amino acids: alanine, asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glutamic acid, glutamine, glycine, proline, serine and tyrosine.
Non-essential does not mean unimportant. It means a dietary supply is not normally required, because the body can make them.
A protein's biological value (its quality as a source of amino acids) depends on whether it supplies all the essential amino acids in the right proportions.
notes.tip: Essential means must come from food, not more important. To differentiate the two, say essential amino acids cannot be made by the body in adequate amounts so must be supplied by food, and non-essential ones are made by the body from other compounds, with a correct named example of each. Lysine and valine are safe essential examples.

notes.h: Peptides and the peptide bond (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Amino acids become proteins by being joined end to end. The link between two amino acids is called a peptide bond.
points: A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group (–COOH) of one amino acid reacts with the amino group (–NH₂) of another. It is not formed between the R groups.
A molecule of water is released in this reaction, so peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction.
The link formed is –CO–NH–.
Two amino acids joined by one peptide bond form a dipeptide. A short chain of amino acids is a peptide, and a long chain is a polypeptide.
A protein is made of one or more polypeptide chains.
Diagram: draw two amino acids side by side, then joined. Label the –CO–NH– link and the molecule of water released.
notes.tip: To describe how a peptide bond forms, name both groups (the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next) and say that water is lost. Do not mix this up with hydrolysis, which uses water.

notes.b: Hydrolysis is the opposite of the reaction that builds protein. It is how long protein chains are broken back into their amino acids.
points: Hydrolysis breaks a peptide bond by adding a molecule of water, which reverses the condensation reaction.
Repeated hydrolysis splits a polypeptide into smaller peptides and finally into free amino acids.
In the body the enzymes pepsin (in the stomach) and trypsin (in the small intestine) do this in digestion. Acid and heat can also hydrolyse protein.
notes.tip: Remember the water: peptide bond formation releases water, while hydrolysis uses it.

keyTerms.definition: A small organic molecule with an amino group and a carboxyl group, which are the building blocks of protein.
The -NH2 group of an amino acid, which carries the nitrogen in protein.
The -COOH group of an amino acid, which gives it its acidic part.
The variable part of an amino acid that distinguishes one amino acid from another.
An amino acid the body cannot make in sufficient amounts, so it must be supplied by the diet.
An amino acid the body can make from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds.
The -CO-NH- link formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, with water released.
The breaking of a chemical bond by adding water, as when peptide bonds are split during digestion.
A long chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

questions.prompt: Name the elements found in protein and identify the four parts of the basic structure of an amino acid.
questions.model: Elements: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, with small amounts of sulphur, phosphorus and iron in some proteins. Protein is the only nutrient containing nitrogen. Amino acid parts: an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable side group (R).

questions.prompt: Describe how two amino acids join to form a peptide bond, and explain how hydrolysis reverses this. Distinguish between essential and non-essential amino acids, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Peptide bond: the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of another, releasing water (condensation); the bond is the -CO-NH- link; two amino acids joined form a dipeptide. Hydrolysis: a molecule of water is added to break the peptide bond, releasing the amino acids; enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin catalyse this in digestion. Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body in sufficient amounts and must be supplied by food; example lysine (eight essential for adults, ten for children). Non-essential amino acids can be made by the body from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds; example alanine. Non-essential does not mean unimportant.
